headline: Highest risk is EMQX’s broad egress interacting with the course repo’s unverified outputs, creating data-leak and cascading-error exposure; prompt-injection and compliance risks are lower.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no runnable surface and no shared channel is documented, while B exposes HTTP API and broad egress. The pairwise injection path is therefore indirect and not default, but if A’s course materials are manually copied into B’s inputs, prompt-like content could influence B. Uncertainty is limited by missing orchestration details, so I keep this low rather than none.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies A-generated text into B’s HTTP API inputs, THEN instruction-like content in that text can influence B.
IF a shared workspace or clipboard is introduced between A and B, THEN prompt injection becomes more plausible.
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate workspaces.
Do not paste A outputs into B without review.
Add a fixed prompt delimiter for any copied text.
Disable B API calls during manual transfer steps.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between tools.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A is docs-only and touches no data classes, but B touches IoT data and has broad network egress plus HTTP API access. If A’s outputs are routed into B, B can transmit that context off-host. The pair does not show a shared filesystem, so this is not high, but the default egress path makes leakage plausible in normal use.
conditions: IF A outputs are fed into B alongside IoT data, THEN B can exfiltrate that combined context over the network.
IF B is configured to send full request context to its backend, THEN any copied A content may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Avoid placing sensitive text from A into B requests.
Redact IoT identifiers before passing data onward.
Use a local-only test dataset.
Review B API payloads before sending.
requires-engineering: enforce field-level egress filtering.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A is not runnable and has no write or network permissions beyond none, while B only shows HTTP API egress. There is no documented overlapping write surface, shared mutable resource, or locking issue. The pairwise conflict pathway is therefore weak and mostly absent unless an external orchestrator adds shared writes not shown here.
conditions: IF an external orchestrator gives both agents write access to the same directory, THEN write conflicts can emerge.
IF B is extended with filesystem or git write permissions, THEN overlap with A-derived artifacts becomes possible.
mitigations: Keep A read-only.
Run B without shared writable mounts.
Separate any generated artifacts by directory.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same files.
requires-engineering: add locking for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A’s outputs are likely instructional content, and B has HTTP API access plus broad egress, so A-to-B handoff can become authoritative if an operator or workflow treats A’s text as ground truth. There is no evidence of verification between them. Because B can act on received content and the interaction is plausible in default workflows, this is medium.
conditions: IF A-generated text is used as input to B without verification, THEN B may propagate A’s errors.
IF B automates downstream actions from received content, THEN mistaken A outputs can cascade into those actions.
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A outputs.
Add a verification checklist for A-derived inputs.
Use a second source to confirm critical facts.
Log provenance for copied content.
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating before action.

E_compliance.rationale: A is an open-source course repo with no data classes touched, while B touches IoT data and has broad egress. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented, so a compliance breach is not established. The only concrete issue is that B could process IoT data in ways A does not constrain, which is a limited gap rather than a clear violation.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is routed through B, THEN its handling must match the operator’s policy.
IF A-derived materials are mixed with regulated data in B, THEN retention and logging controls must be checked.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B unless approved.
Review B retention settings.
Separate training/course content from production data.
Document data flow boundaries.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for regulated classes.
